narrative:
The model estimated a 62.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty: among applicants with a similar profile, roughly 63 in 100 failed first time. Because that estimate crossed the school’s risk cutoff, your application was denied.

The denial was driven most strongly by your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest tenth of your class, while accepted students averaged around the sixth tenth; this was the single largest push toward a failure prediction. Your first-year class standing, also the lowest tenth versus an accepted average near the sixth tenth, was the third most influential factor and likewise pushed toward failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score. At 39, it was slightly above the accepted average of 37.18, so it pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the concern raised by your class standing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, below the accepted average of 3.23, may also reinforce the academic-risk picture, though it was not among the top three drivers. Gender and race were not used.

To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback, consider retaking the LSAT only if practice tests show meaningful improvement, and strengthen your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a graduate program. Reapply when you can show a clearer upward trend and evidence that the earlier academic pattern does not reflect your current preparation.
